section_summary: This section contains State Department records from 1938 to 1944 focusing on Japanese governmental organization, cabinet changes, wartime administrative centralization, and anti-militarist movements. Prominent topics include the emergence of the Jushin (senior statesmen) council to replace the Genro, total-war industrial reorganizations including the Armament Ministry and Supreme War Directing Council, and the political fallout of Allied victories culminating in the fall of the Tojo Cabinet. The file also chronicles activities of anti-fascist Japanese groups in the United States and the Chinese Communist base of Yenan, notably the Japanese American Committee for Democracy and Susumu Okano's Japanese People's Emancipation League.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a Tokyo despatch concerning the establishment of Japan's new Genro advisory body.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Despatch No. 4917 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. It notes the report on a new advisory body replacing the old Genro institution for selecting Japanese prime ministers. The original paper was filed under 894.00/961.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Japan's New Genro

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report analyzing the emergence of the Jushin council of senior statesmen replacing the Genro in selecting Japanese prime ministers.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits an analytical report based partly on an article by Dr. Masamichi Royama in Contemporary Japan. The despatch reviews how the assassination of Premier Inukai in 1932 and military aggression in Manchuria ended party government and diminished the role of Prince Saionji, the last surviving Genro. It explains the development of the Jushin body, composed of the Lord Privy Seal, the President of the Privy Council, and former prime ministers, who now deliberate on cabinet selections under significant military influence.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4917: Japan's New Genro

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting conversations regarding Japanese-Chinese peace negotiations and domestic cabinet instability.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 1171 concerning negotiations with the Chungking Government for recognition of the Wang Ching-wei regime. It references conversations held by Dr. Charles B. Fahs with Japanese officials, during which Mr. Ushiba suggested a government change might occur and attributed the German pact entirely to Konoye and Matsuoka.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Negotiations with Chungking Govt for Recognition of Wang Ching Wei Govt

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording diplomatic observations on the political uncertainty of the Konoye Government.
subfiles.summary: This sheet indexes Telegram No. 1039 from the American Embassy in Vichy regarding conversations with French diplomat Jean Chauvel and information from Ambassador Charles Arsène-Henry in Tokyo. It highlights the prevailing political instability in Tokyo and the difficulty of identifying a plausible successor to Prince Konoye.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Government of Japan

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum comparing the administrative abilities and civil service backgrounds of Japanese and American public officials.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine elaborates on his view that Japanese public figures generally compare unfavorably in ability with their American counterparts despite an elite competitive examination system. He attributes this disparity to a less varied life experience, educational narrowness, and an uncompetitive bureaucratic tenure once appointed. He notes, however, that Japanese officials possess high devotion to the national interest, tact, and tenacity, citing Prince Saionji and Takashi Hara as rare exceptions of brilliant statesmanship.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Comparative Ability of Japanese and American Public Officials

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet regarding rumored disagreements within the Japanese Cabinet over the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet indexes Tokyo Telegram No. 765 concerning rumors of a policy split between Prime Minister Konoye and Foreign Minister Matsuoka. It notes a message from Japanese official Matsumoto denying the cleavage and clarifying Tokyo's policy on the Tripartite Treaty.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Rumored Cleavage Between Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum analyzing Axis recognition of the Wang Ching-wei puppet regime in Nanking.
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck argues that German and Italian diplomatic recognition of the Wang Ching-wei regime will not benefit Japan among the Chinese populace. He highlights Italy's explicit admission that recognition was granted at the request of the Japanese Government, publicly confirming Wang's subordinate puppet status. Hornbeck concludes that both supporters of Nanking and Chungking will view this subservience as an insult to Chinese pride.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: German and Italian Recognition of Wang Ching-wei

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet documenting high-level departmental discussions on a newly formed Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference note records a telephone conversation between Maxwell M. Hamilton and the Secretary of State regarding the new government set up in Japan. The original memorandum is filed under decimal 711.94/2178-9/18.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: New Government Set Up by Japanese

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet reporting the resignation of the Japanese Ambassador to the Soviet Union and the designation of his successor.
subfiles.summary: This note indexes Telegram No. 1188 from the American Embassy in the U.S.S.R. reporting the resignation of Ambassador Yoshitsugu Tatekawa on February 28, 1942. It states that Tatekawa is to be succeeded as Ambassador to Moscow by Naotake Sato, counselor in the Foreign Office.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Resignation of Japanese Ambassador Tatekawa

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet concerning press statements on petroleum export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: This sheet indexes a memorandum requesting revisions to two proposed press releases on petroleum product export controls. It notes that the restrictions should be justified by American defense needs while avoiding specific mention of Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Restrictions on Exports of Petroleum Products

subfiles.about: Letter acknowledging the receipt of informational pamphlets concerning Japan.
subfiles.summary: George Atcheson, Jr., Assistant Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledges with thanks the receipt of three pamphlets concerning Japan submitted to the Department by Juanita Miller of Los Angeles.
subfiles.title: Letter to Juanita Miller Acknowledging Pamphlets on Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing material on Japanese industrial reorganization and rationalization.
subfiles.summary: This note indexes a letter concerning the 'Rational Plan for the Reorganization of Japan' and the Japanese Government's study of industrial rationalization. The original paper is filed under 894.20/280.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Rational Plan for the Reorganization of Japan

subfiles.about: Telegraphic resolution of loyalty to the United States sent by Japanese American citizens in Oregon.
subfiles.from: Portland Chapter, Japanese American Citizens League
subfiles.summary: The Portland Chapter of the Japanese American Citizens League transmits a resolution adopted at a patriotic rally on January 23, 1942. The assembled residents reaffirm their loyalty to the United States and pledge their services and resources to defeat Japan and its Axis partners.
subfiles.title: Telegram: JACL Patriotic Rally Resolution of Loyalty

subfiles.about: Correspondence between the Japanese American Committee for Democracy and the State Department regarding anti-fascist coordination.
subfiles.summary: Yoshitaka Takagi writes to Harold B. Hoskins commending the State Department's participation in a conference held by the American Committee for Protection of Foreign Born in Cleveland and offering the JACD's cooperation in the war effort. On May 21, Hoskins replies thanking Takagi for his letter and the enclosed JACD News Letter and expressing gratitude for the offer of assistance.
subfiles.title: Correspondence Between JACD and Executive Assistant Hoskins

subfiles.about: Internal memoranda and correspondence concerning a testimonial letter of loyalty presented to the President by the JACD.
subfiles.from: Toshi Aline Ohta / Division of Protocol / Edwin M. Watson
subfiles.summary: This dossier documents the handling of a testimonial of loyalty sent to President Roosevelt by Toshi Aline Ohta on behalf of the Japanese American Committee for Democracy. The White House referred the document to the State Department, where the Division of Far Eastern Affairs and Division of Protocol recommended a presidential acknowledgment. The file concludes with a draft and signed acknowledgment from Major General Edwin M. Watson, Secretary to the President, expressing appreciation for the testimonial.
subfiles.title: Dossier: JACD Testimonial of Loyalty and Presidential Acknowledgment

subfiles.about: Military intelligence request for State Department documentation on Japanese military government administration in the Dutch East Indies.
subfiles.summary: Lt. Colonel W. M. Adams of the Military Intelligence Service requests State Department data for the School of Military Government at Charlottesville, Virginia. The school seeks details regarding Japanese administrative, fiscal, and economic practices in occupied territories, especially the Dutch East Indies. State Department officers are asked to furnish relevant reports through liaison channels.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Japanese Military Government in Japanese-held Territory

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum on the de facto structure of the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: This sheet indexes a memorandum prepared by John K. Emmerson entitled 'Japan's Govt. in Fact.' The original memorandum is filed under decimal 740.0011 Pacific War/2037.7/8.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Japan's Govt. in Fact

subfiles.about: Correspondence and memorandum discussing a proposal to distribute a Japanese translation of Joseph C. Grew's book in Brazil.
subfiles.from: Yoshitaka Takagi / Allan Dawson / John C. Dreier
subfiles.summary: Yoshitaka Takagi of the JACD informs the State Department of plans to publish a Japanese translation of former Ambassador Grew's 'Report from Tokyo' and asks whether it can be distributed among Japanese immigrants in Brazil. State Department officer Allan Dawson advises against official U.S. promotion of the book in Brazil, suggesting instead that the JACD contact Brazilian Japanese groups directly. Assistant Chief John C. Dreier subsequently writes to Takagi suggesting he consult the Brazilian Consulate in New York.
subfiles.title: Correspondence: Distribution of 'Report from Tokyo' Translation in Brazil

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram and paraphrase assessing Premier Tojo's announced wartime emergency measures and Allied strategic pressures.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Winant conveys British Foreign Office views regarding sweeping domestic measures announced in Tokyo by Premier Tojo. British officials do not foresee an immediate tactical change or government collapse, but view the steps as a reaction to Italy's surrender, setbacks in New Guinea and the Aleutians, and the formation of the South East Asia Command. The analysis observes that Japanese official rhetoric has shifted from imperial expansion to desperate defense of the home islands and Manchukuo.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 6380: British Foreign Office Analysis of Tojo Emergency Measures

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram detailing German reports on Japanese wartime administrative reorganization and the creation of an Armament Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Minister Leland Harrison reports German news releases concerning major Japanese administrative shifts, notably the creation of a centralized Armament Ministry absorbing armament procurement from other ministries. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry is slated to be replaced by a Commerce and Agriculture Ministry to manage resources across continental Asia. The dispatch highlights the replacement of civilian bureaucrats by army and navy officers and mentions Helmuth Wohlthat's survey of Japanese-occupied China based on German industrial methods.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 6381: Japanese Administrative Changes and Armament Ministry

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting German editorial commentary on the leadership of the new Japanese Armament Ministry and Nobusuke Kishi.
subfiles.summary: Harrison transmits German commentary on the consolidation of Japanese war industry through merging the Planning Bureau and the Economics Ministry into the Armament Ministry. The report discusses candidates for minister, including Lt. Gen. Teiichi Suzuki and Admiral Teijiro Toyoda, noting that Nobusuke Kishi will serve as Deputy Minister and guiding personality. Because Japanese tradition bars a civilian from outranking senior military collaborators, Premier Tojo or another high-ranking officer is expected to hold the formal portfolio.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 6529: German Commentary on Japanese Armament Ministry and Kishi

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram transmitting German press accounts of new Japanese legislation creating industrial 'production generals.'
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports German accounts of new legislation passed by the Japanese Diet holding armament companies and designated individuals, termed 'production generals,' directly responsible for war production. Deputy Minister Kishi testified that these appointees would typically be company presidents appointed by imperial decree to streamline production and eliminate bureaucratic impediments. The Armament Ministry assumes supreme control over prices, capital financing, accounting, and labor allocation for munitions manufacturing.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 7264: Japanese Armament Legislation and Production Generals

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram summarizing German press reports on the internal reorganization of Japan's Greater East Asia Ministry.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports on German coverage of the structural reshuffle of the Greater East Asia Ministry effective December 1, 1943. The ministry incorporated commercial and industrial functions from dissolved ministries, creating an Industrial Department and restructuring its General, Manchurian, Chinese, and Southern Overseas departments. The revisions aim to tighten administration, eliminate redundant sections, and enforce stricter continental price and enterprise controls.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 7877: Reorganization of Greater East Asia Ministry

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting Tojo's directives to major Japanese war industries and a major wartime tax increase.
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports Japanese press coverage of Premier Tojo's instructions to 150 leading industrial firms in aviation, shipping, steel, oil, and machine building to name responsible managers under the new armament law within two weeks. Tojo emphasized priority concentration on aircraft production and mutual industrial cooperation. In parallel, the government announced a new tax program designed to raise two billion yen from one million newly taxed citizens.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 502: Tojo Directives to Armament Industries and New Tax Program

subfiles.about: Military intelligence follow-up requesting a consular dispatch on Japanese military government methods.
subfiles.summary: Lt. Colonel W. M. Adams of G-2 requests a copy of Consul General Walter A. Foote's dispatch No. 15 of January 14, 1943, concerning Japanese military government methods. The document is sought to support training curricula at the School of Military Government in Charlottesville, Virginia.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Despatch Desired by School of Military Government

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum proposing policy options should the Japanese Emperor flee to the Asian continent and abdicate.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine suggests text additions to a policy memorandum for Joseph C. Grew regarding the contingency of the Japanese Emperor abandoning the homeland for continental China or Manchuria. He proposes declaring that such a flight constitutes voluntary abdication, allowing Allied occupation authorities either to enthrone another imperial family member or abolish the throne depending on Japanese public opinion. He highlights the immense psychological propaganda value of framing the flight as desertion of the Japanese people.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Proposed Policy on Contingency of Emperor's Flight

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum warning of the possible flight of the Japanese imperial court and high command to China.
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary Breckinridge Long brings to Joseph C. Grew's attention the contingency that the Japanese High Command, civilian authorities, and Royal Family might flee Japan for inland China as Allied forces approach the home islands. He warns that large continental army units and puppet regimes around Peking and Nanking could provide a formidable redoubt, urging contingency planning by Far Eastern specialists.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Contingency of Japanese Flight to Continental China

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting British press analysis on the fall of the Tojo Cabinet and appointment of Koiso and Yonai.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Winant summarizes British newspaper commentary, particularly from The Times, Daily Telegraph, and Manchester Guardian, regarding the fall of General Tojo following the defeat at Saipan. The joint selection of General Kuniaki Koiso and Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai is viewed as evidence of sharp inter-service conflict and Kwantung Army militarism. Press dispatches emphasize severe shipping losses, declining air power, and the psychological impact on the Japanese public of shifting from imperial conquests to home defense.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 5814: British Press Commentary on Tojo's Fall and New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting leadership changes in the Imperial Rule Assistance Political Association.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Harriman transmits a Tokyo press dispatch stating that Admiral Seizo Kobayashi has agreed to serve as president of the Imperial Rule Assistance Political Association. Kobayashi replaces General Nobuyuki Abe, who resigned the leadership post following his appointment as Governor General of Korea.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 2911: Leadership Change in Imperial Rule Assistance Association

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum and press clipping analyzing the formation of Japan's Supreme War Directing Council.
subfiles.summary: H. Merrell Benninghoff critiques a Washington Star column by Japanese journalist K. K. Kawakami, who argued that the newly created Supreme War Directing Council was an attempt by the military clique to shift blame for defeat onto civilian moderates. Benninghoff clarifies that the Council directly supersedes the consultative Liaison Council to bridge the structural gap between the civil government and the Supreme Command. He concludes that the Koiso Cabinet created the council to enforce centralized efficiency and maximize the total war effort rather than prepare for surrender.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: The Japanese Supreme War Directing Council

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting an observer report on the Japanese People's Emancipation League at Yenan and a speech by Susumu Okano.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Gauss transmits Report No. 12 prepared by Second Secretary John S. Service of the U.S. Army Observer Section at Yenan, along with the text of an address delivered on August 12, 1944, by Japanese Communist leader Susumu Okano (Sanzo Nosaka). Service notes that the League consists primarily of indoctrinated Japanese prisoners of war aiding the 18th Group Army. Okano appeals for Allied recognition and collaboration, detailing potential anti-militarist forces within Japan and outlining plans for a post-war democratic republic.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2981: Report on Japanese People's Emancipation League at Yenan

subfiles.about: Military headquarters despatch transmitting Service's report and Okano's Yenan address to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: John Paton Davies, Jr., detailed to USAF-CBI headquarters, forwards John S. Service's Report No. 12 on the Japanese People's Emancipation League to ensure Department receipt. Davies characterizes the League as the only significant 'Free Japan' movement in existence and urges close study of its potential for Allied invasion planning and post-war governance. Attached is the full text of Okano's speech welcoming American observers and urging common action against Japanese militarism.
subfiles.title: Despatch: Transmitting Report on Japanese People's Emancipation League

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting a proposal from Susumu Okano to the JACD in New York to form a unified Japanese people's front.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires a.i. Arthur R. Ringwalt forwards a letter from Susumu Okano in Yenan addressed to Yoshitaka Takagi of the Japanese American Committee for Democracy in New York. Okano proposes establishing a joint committee of democratic Japanese and Japanese Americans, offering to locate the League's headquarters in the United States to broaden its international backing beyond Chinese Communist territory. John Paton Davies comments that this gesture reflects an effort to invite American influence over organized democratic movements in post-war Japan.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3160: Transmission of Letter from Susumu Okano to JACD

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing an article on Korea for the Harvard Civil Affairs Training School.
subfiles.summary: This note indexes correspondence enclosing an article on Korea by Hugh Borton intended for military government officers at Harvard University's Civil Affairs Training School. The original item is filed under 895.01A/12-1144.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Article on Korea for Harvard CATS
subfiles.to: Civil Affairs Training School, Harvard University

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Hugh Borton's study on Korean internal political structure.
subfiles.summary: This sheet indexes a letter from Northwestern University enclosing Hugh Borton's paper on the internal political structure of Korea. The original document is filed under decimal 895.01/12-1144.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Article on Korea Internal Political Structure

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum recommending the disapproval of Japanese naval inspector assignments to Los Angeles.
subfiles.summary: Cabot Coville reviews notifications and tax-exemption requests from the Japanese Embassy regarding three Japanese naval personnel assigned from New York to Los Angeles. Citing Navy Department objections and public hostility toward alien military agents, Coville recommends rejecting the expansion of Japanese naval offices beyond New York City and drafting a reply denying the desired income tax exemptions.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Japanese Naval Inspector's Office Personnel in Los Angeles

subfiles.about: Departmental memorandum summarizing records of foreign military and naval purchasing missions in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Coville summarizes Division of Controls records on foreign military purchasing and inspection offices with fixed locations in the United States, listing Japan, France, Great Britain, and Australia. He also enumerates 28 countries maintaining traveling purchasing missions without fixed addresses, noting that reporting such missions to the State Department is voluntary.
subfiles.title: Memorandum: Foreign Military and Naval Offices in the United States
